title: What's the future of the Democratic party in Texas, amid historic midterm wins?
description: NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a Democrat, about Texas flipping blue and what it means for future elections.
body:
NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a Democrat, about Texas flipping blue and what it means for future elections.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  OK. We're going to go now to somebody with a long history being in the minority when it comes to Texas politics. Democrat Wendy Davis, a former Texas state senator. Welcome.WENDY DAVIS: Thank you. I'm so happy to be on with you today.CHANG: So happy to have you. I want to start 12 years ago because you yourself ran for governor of Texas as a Democrat in 2014. You ran against Greg Abbott, and you lost by 20 points. And then this year, we see Democrat Gina Hinojosa also run against Greg Abbott. And she wins by this pretty comfortable margin, by about seven points. How surprised were you by that result?DAVIS: Surprised by the degree to which she won. But I've been part of Gina's team from the jump and was privileged to be seeing the data as we were looking at what was coming in on the early vote and testing that against the way the model had been built to determine, you know, whether Gina would be ahead.CHANG: Yeah.DAVIS: And we felt really good going into Election Day that she was positioned to win. And unless there had been some huge, unexpected turnout by Republicans that day, we felt like she was going to win. But the fact that she won by the margin that she won by.CHANG: Yeah.DAVIS: The fact that every statewide race underneath her was also one that a Democrat won, that we won state Supreme Court races, but also another very near and dear project to my heart, which has been to raise money for and invest in down ballot races. We flipped 21 state House seats last night.CHANG: And the question I have is, why do you think that was? I mean, we just heard my colleague, Ashley Lopez, talk a little bit about this. But what do you think changed between your run 12 years ago and today...DAVIS: Yeah.CHANG: ...To allow for such a different result against the same Republican candidate, at least in the governor's race, Greg Abbott?DAVIS: Yeah, I mean, if you go back to 2014, it was a year of tremendous complacency by Democrats, a similar complacency to what we saw from Republicans this cycle. And there's no question that this year was an absolute repudiation of Trump and his agenda, and the fact that Greg Abbott and other state leaders had absolutely traded what had been considered their prior more traditional conservative values for MAGA. And they had leaned so hard into that. But for Greg Abbott particularly, he had leaned very hard into the cruelty of the Trump immigration agenda. And he paid a price for that last night.CHANG: So it sounds like you - it sounds like what you're saying is last night, in Texas at least, it was more of a repudiation against Trump and Abbott and less about Democrats hitting on a different kind of message to Texans this time around?DAVIS: No. No, I don't want to leave that impression at all. The repudiation piece was part of it. But our Democrats offered something that I think was incredibly unique and pitch perfect. And I'll use Gina as the example of this. Gina knew from the outset what she wanted to deliver for the people of Texas. She gave, consistently throughout, a message of understanding the pain that they were feeling economically, really leaning into, in a very experienced and empathetic way, what was happening to their public schools and the loss of opportunity, the fact that so many people in our state don't have healthcare. And...CHANG: But if I may.DAVIS: Yes.CHANG: If I may, I want to talk about you and just...DAVIS: Yeah.CHANG: ...If you would like, to give you your flowers, because your name has been popping up a lot next to the name of Beto O'Rourke. As two Texas Democrats who tried to pave the way, do you feel like you helped build the momentum that we saw crest last night into this blue wave in Texas in about...DAVIS: I think...CHANG: ...Twenty seconds or so (laughter).DAVIS: I think every person that runs and, you know, raises resources and energizes voters helps to build the path for the people that come afterward. Beto did better than I did. And now Gina, of course, has crested that mountain. And I couldn't be more proud to have played a role in helping that along and staying involved. And that's what Beto did, too.CHANG: All right.DAVIS: Neither of us have given up on our state and we never will.CHANG: That is Democrat Wendy Davis, former Texas state Senator. Thank you.DAVIS: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party
body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a midterm election night watch party at the Department at Hudson's on November 4 in Detroit, Michigan.
                
                    Salwan Georges/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salwan Georges/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   Democrats coasted into victory late last night, taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate by considerable margins. Several states that are traditionally characterized as "deep red," including Texas, Kansas and Iowa, flipped towards Democrats in the Senate for the first time in decades. Democratic candidates also took a convincing majority in House races, despite competing in several states whose districts were redrawn to favor Republicans.   Across the country, Democratic gubernatorial candidates also burst ahead, winning races in GOP strongholds like Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Heading into 2027, Democrats will officially retake control of Congress and hold at least 28 governorships.   
   Newly elected Democratic officials, party leaders and pollsters joined Morning Edition on Wednesday morning to share their insights on the massive wave of Democratic victories in state and local races. In their interviews with NPR's Steve Inskeep and Michel Martin, these Democrats discussed takeaways from the midterm results, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, the mandate received from voters and the next steps for the party. You can read some key takeaways from the discussions below.    Abdul El-Sayed   Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate as Democrats retake control of Congress. He said his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, campaigned weaponizing El-Sayed's name and faith rather than addressing issues Americans really care about, like Medicare for All and the price of everyday items.   El-Sayed also discussed his opinions on legislation surrounding the war in Iran, and he agreed with Trump's scheduled end to roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel.   Martin asked him about his lack of support from some Jewish and Black voters, something El Sayed said he hopes to remedy.   "There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.   To listen to Abdul El-Sayed's full Morning Edition interview, click here.   
   Eric Holder   Eric Holder, chairman of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee and attorney general under former President Obama, discussed how mid-decade redistricting affected the results of the midterm. Speaking with Martin, he said that GOP gerrymandering efforts backfired, causing candidates to lose in districts that were specifically drawn for their success.   "The redistricting efforts that [Republicans] had didn't just fail — they were dismantled," Holder says.   To listen to Eric Holder's full Morning Edition interview, click here.   Stacey Abrams   Democrats in Georgia won seats up and down the ballot, and Stacey Abrams, founder of Fair Fight Action, said the party has been building towards this outcome since 2010. In her interview with Martin, she added that she's proud of Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman elected governor in United States history. Abrams campaigned for the same gubernatorial spot in 2018 and again in 2020, though she was never elected to the position.   Abrams said Democratic victories for the governor, attorney general, secretary of state and in the state house "gives us an opportunity to start correcting and restoring rights that we've seen lost across the South for more than 20 years."    To listen to Stacey Abram's full Morning Edition interview, click here.   Ken Martin   Ken Martin, chairman of the Democratic National Committee, said yesterday's election marks the biggest win for his party in more than a century. Voters gave Democrats a mandate to address affordability, health care and the systems that exclusively benefit wealthy Americans, he explained to Martin and Inskeep, and he thinks newly elected Democrats can deliver.   "Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he said. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."   To listen to Ken Martin's full Morning Edition interview, click here.    Margie Omero   Pollster and Democratic strategist Margie Omero explained why last night's results are a direct reflection of voter's distrust of leaders in Washington. She said contested races consistently broke towards Democrats, despite high GOP spending during campaign season.   
   "Voters really wanted to send a real clear message, and they couldn't have been any clearer than what we heard last night," Omero said.   To listen to Margie Omero's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

title: Chuck Schumer heralds Democrats' 'generational remake' of Senate
description: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-
body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, DC, on Nov. 4, 2026.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."    "These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," the New York Democrat said outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they — the American people — want."   Democrats secured major gains in red states President Trump has previously carried, including Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Their victories include a history-making win in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.    
   Schumer, who is poised to become Senate Majority leader in January, credited these wins to a crop of candidates who "knew how to tailor their message to the states."   Democrats now have a 54-seat majority, including the two independent senators who caucus with the party. Two races have still not been called: Alaska and Mississippi.     Schumer vowed that "relief is on the way" for voters, and acknowledged that some remain skeptical that Democrats will deliver. He said Democrats are intent on bringing down the cost of living, ending the Iran war, and undertaking investigations into the White House to address allegations of corruption.    "The days of Trump's supplicant Senate are over," Schumer declared.    President Trump hasn't shied away from saying he will use his veto pen on Democratic legislative priorities, but has also signaled some openness to cutting deals with the new Democratic-controlled Congress.    "We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him," Schumer said.     Loading...

title: Navajo voters hop tractors, make extraordinary efforts to vote after widespread flooding
description: Lilien Begay, 92, seated at left with da
body:
Lilien Begay, 92, seated at left with daughters (clockwise) Berneice, Darlene, and Vera at the voting site in Denehotso, Arizona on Nov. 3, 2026
                
                    Adam Burke/KSUT
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Adam Burke/KSUT
    

   
   People on the Navajo Reservation had to make extra effort to vote this year.   It's a region of the southwest that's been hit this fall by repeated flooding. Roads washed out, driving thousands of people from their homes.   But voters turned out, in the parts of Arizona, Utah and New Mexico that the reservation stretches across. Yesterday at the Dennehotso Chapterhouse, voters rolled up in trucks with mud-caked tires.   The town is framed by the picturesque sandstone cursive of Comb Ridge, the stone spires of Monument Valley peeking over the ridgeline.   In the parking lot, people gathered to eat fry bread and mutton stew, something common at Navajo polling sites.   
   "I love to see our people come out and talk amongst each other," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie, adding that this year's election is unusual.   "People are having to drive on tractors to get from one road to another, just to come and vote," she said.   Dennehotso has been knocked around by floods this fall, three in the last month. But the big one that residents will talk about for decades to come, started on October 22.   Local contractor Kev Woolboy was helping coordinate response efforts, checking watersheds along the highway, as floodwaters from as far as 60 miles away raced toward town.   "We have some man-made earth dams that were supposed to slow (the water) down," Woolboy said. "But there was so much rain, those earth dams didn't stand a chance."   The floodwaters ravaged homes and newly-built roads, knocking out power and water, and leaving part of the town covered in thick, goopy mud.   "We thought we were safe," said 74-year-old Phyllis Yazzie.   Yazzie was at home with her son that day, having a late breakfast, when her niece called.   "And she says, 'Auntie! You better get out of there!'" Yazzie recalled. "I said, 'Why?' And she says, 'the flood's heading that way.' And so I went outside, I started looking towards the wash, and I saw the water rising.'"   
   They tried to drive out their dirt road, but were forced back to the highest point on their land, while a torrent of water carved ravines on both sides of their house.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Kev Woolboy at the home of Phyllis Yazzie, and elderly woman he helped rescue from flooding
                
                    Adam Burke/KSUT
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Adam Burke/KSUT
    

   
   "We parked the car and we spent the night in the vehicle," Yazzie said. "But they were trying to rescue us."   While Yazzie and her son huddled in their car, Kev Woolboy was working his way toward them, as the local guide for the Navajo Police Department, who had brought in an amphibious vehicle to rescue residents.   "I was jumping into the water and bringing the kids and some of the elders on board and helping them with their personal belongings," Woolboy said.   As it grew dark, and the flood waters rose, Woolboy says it became impossible to tell the difference between the ground and a swirling mix of rainfall and reddish brown silt.   They got close to Phyllis Yazzie's house, Woolboy asked the officers to stop the vehicle.   "I told the guys something doesn't look right," Woolboy recalled. "So they turned on their floodlights to where I could see. There was no road there. We had to turn around, we couldn't get Phyllis that night."   Two weeks later, residents were still digging out. On election day, a backhoe was building a a temporary road so that residents cut off from town could reach the polls at the Chapterhouse   Volunteer drivers, and Chapter employees were shuttling people there, too. Some people drove hours to get there.   Vera Begay was there, with her 92-year-old mother Lilien Begay, who lost her home and all of her identification documents.   "She's never missed her vote- all her life she's come here for voting," said Vera Begay.   The elder Begay, speaking in Navajo, said she is emotionally devastated.   This year in Dennehoto, and across the region, flooding has brought out the best in communities.   
   "It means a lot more to our people to come out and vote," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie. "Because this is a very very important time to do so, especially with the flood and all that's happening all over the Navajo Nation. It's tough out here."   But on election day, people who may disagree about politics were laughing and crying together, bringing their community back to life.

title: Democrats sweeping victories mean big changes for Trump's final two years in office
description:
Transcript
        
    MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  Today is a day for all of the superlatives. Unbelievable, unprecedented, st
body:
Transcript
        
    MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  Today is a day for all of the superlatives. Unbelievable, unprecedented, stunning - just a few of the words being used to describe Democratic victories across the country in midterm elections.AILSA CHANG, HOST:  And just to recap, Democrats won majorities in both houses of Congress, picking up at least seven seats in the Senate. Two races in Mississippi and Alaska are still too close to call. Democrats also took control of the House, flipping more than two dozen seats, with races yet to be called.KELLY: They also picked up five governorships. They captured control of at least nine state legislative houses. So how did they do it? And what might Democratic control of Congress look like? Those are a couple of the questions I'm going to put now to NPR White House correspondent Emily Feng, congressional reporter Eric McDaniel and senior political editor and correspondent Domenico Montanaro. We got a whole team here. Domenico, I'm going to throw you the question that I had waking up this morning. Did the Democrats win or did the Republicans lose?DOMENICO MONTANARO, BYLINE: Yeah, it's not really an either-or. Clearly, the overriding factor, though, was Donald Trump. I mean, his unpopularity, the war in Iran, rising prices, the growing gap between the uber-rich and the middle class. I mean, some $12 billion spent on this election while other people are struggling to buy gas. All of that together created a huge backlash, maybe call it a Trump-lash. Democrats, though, also did recruit very good candidates. You don't win in places like Iowa, Texas, Kansas as Democrats without candidates who can make the most of the moment and be good fits for their states. They showed real level of authenticity. That will give them a big opportunity to show what Democrats did wasn't just a big midterm asterisk.KELLY: And one more to you, Domenico, because we've been talking a lot, you and I, about polling these last few weeks. Were the polls going to work? Could we trust them? In the end, they did all right.MONTANARO: In the end, they did do OK. You know, they pointed in the right direction. If anything, they underestimated Democratic support. But we don't know how many people decided late, you know, after when the polls had been conducted before the election. And things usually do break in one direction in midterms. It happened in 2006. It happened again in this election. Polls predicted Democrats plus 8 on the generic congressional ballot. It wound up being bigger, closer to plus 13, which is massive and no one would have believed it beforehand. Even with the underestimation, all the signs were there for a pretty big wave with what the polls were showing, but people were rightfully cautious given the polling errors we've seen over the past decade that had underestimated Republican support.KELLY: Yeah.MONTANARO: It's just very difficult in this age, when there's been such a major political realignment, to poll.KELLY: Eric McDaniel, you cover Congress.ERIC MCDANIEL, BYLINE: Indeed, I do.KELLY: Lucky you. Here's my question to you. What happens immediately? Because Republicans still control the House and the Senate for the next couple months. Does anything change between now and January?MCDANIEL: Well, I mean, it only gets harder for Republicans, right? They've got a narrow majority right now in the House, a small majority in the Senate. But good luck to them getting every one of those folks who lost back into Washington to pass legislation on a party-line basis. There's not a lot of incentive...KELLY: Yeah.MCDANIEL: ...To come back to town. And that's important stuff. That's government funding. That's more money for the Iran war. They also have to figure out what their leadership looks like next. Our friend Barbara Sprunt is reporting that current Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, he won't seek reelection as the top House Republican. That sets up a battle between at least two folks, Jim Jordan of Ohio and Steve Scalise of Louisiana. Jim Jordan's pugnacious. He's a brawler. He could be dispositionally well suited to counter Democrats' investigation-heavy agenda. Scalise is sort of a party man. He's a committed Trump ally, but generally seen as less pugnacious than Jordan.But - and this is speculation on my part - I think there's probably an appetite for someone willing to take a more Trump-skeptical stance as a party leader - right? - given the mollywhopping voters just delivered the party because of the president.KELLY: Yeah. And then agenda? I mean, how do we expect Democrats are going to use their newfound majorities come January?MCDANIEL: They'll act on the things they campaigned on. That's cost of living. That's perceived political corruption. They talk about cost of living from healthcare to housing. But with Trump still in the White House, I don't expect that those bills will absolutely become law. In perceived public corruption, expect bills on lawmaker stock trading and then investigations into investigations into investigations - every part of Trump's life from his administration's agenda and the extent of his relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The likely incoming House oversight chair, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, posted on Twitter last night, simply, lawyer up.KELLY: Lawyer up. Sounds ominous. Emily Feng, hop in here. What's the mood at the White House like today?EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Yeah, so I am at the White House today. It's quiet, but it's also surreal, and that's because the president has had one public event so far today, and it was not about the election. It was to talk about his East Wing ballroom construction project. He had hundreds of construction workers who were building it come in. And at this event, he spent most of his time talking about the quality of the marble that he was using and his new helipad and really not about the election. However, last night, a White House official told NPR that the mood watching these results come in was, quote, "defiant at the White House." And then today, Trump's Truth Social media account shared a picture of a red hat with the word veto written on it because Trump has said he is going to veto most bills brought to him by a Democratic Congress.More broadly, the sense I get is the mood in the Republican Party is one of confusion and of soul searching. As my colleagues have just pointed out, these midterms were a big rebuke of Trump himself. He has been quick to point out he was not literally on the ballot, but voters rejected his policies, you know, his economic policies and tariffs, the war in Iran. And even his own vice president today, JD Vance, broke with Trump and wrote on X that he thinks one of the primary reasons behind Republican losses was the war in Iran. So today, when Trump was celebrating, you know, the last steel ceiling beam that was being put in place in the ballroom project, reporters asked him if he regretted, perhaps, the Iran war costing the GOP the House and the Senate, and he said this.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Probably it's true, but at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.KELLY: Interesting. So, I mean, Emily, is there any sign, any indication that President Trump might be willing to change course with the war in Iran?FENG: He seemed to soften his stance a little today. He said today he could end the war, quote, "anytime" he wanted. He said last night on Fox & Friends that he would still strike Iran, though, if Iran, quote, "does not behave." But also that the two countries could have a diplomatic ending to this, that they could sign something to end the war. He has warned that any new major strikes would happen after the midterms, but he's already said he will not use nuclear weapons. He told Politico last night he does not need to use nuclear weapons against Iran.KELLY: Eric, back to you. One of the outgrowths of the war in Iran has, of course, been high diesel prices, high gas prices. Affordability, affordability, affordability, which was a huge factor in the election, we're told.MCDANIEL: Such a huge factor.KELLY: Yeah. I mean, can congressional Democrats do much about that? Can they bring prices down when they aren't going to control the White House for at least two years?MCDANIEL: I mean, let's see, right? Democrats can send bills to the president's desk, but they can't make him sign. That said, they can make a real stink about the fact that they've made changes they say would be positive for the American people and that the president is, say, standing in their way. That kind of public pressure could matter. The president wants to be liked. He's signaled some openness to dealmaking. And there's leverage, like government funding, getting rid of the filibuster, confirming the president's picks to various posts, that could help grease the wheels of dealmaking. But it's not going to be easy for Democrats, but I don't want to pretend like movement is impossible either.KELLY: Do Democrats feel like they have a mandate? Did voters give them a mandate?MCDANIEL: I mean, I don't know that there is such a thing as a mandate in today's political environment, right? This was about the president - 38% approval rating, 70% of the public peeved about the war in Iran. Gas prices up 40% year over year. Democrats had the right message about how to address it, but their favorability rating as a party is still minus 14. Chuck Schumer's among the most disliked men in America. Domenico can talk about this more, but last night saw huge swings across demographics, groups that had swung to President Trump in 2024. And so now Democrats have to do the hard work convincing those folks to stay in their corner. This isn't a captured electorate, by any means.KELLY: Yeah, this is the problem, Domenico - right? - with you win an election, and you inherit the problems and they become yours. What risks come with these wins for Democrats?MONTANARO: Yeah, I mean, right now, Democrats are the dog that caught the car. So can they drive, right? I mean, they can do a lot of things here. They can block judges and cabinet members. They can stop Trump's legislative agenda, whatever that winds up being, if he would have wanted to do anything. But they really have to be careful on how they message this and not to overpromise and underdeliver. I mean, that's something voters have become all too familiar with from politicians in Washington.The reality is it's unlikely Democrats are going to have a real good-faith negotiating partner in Republicans in trying to get big things done. And it's looking like Donald Trump is not wanting to be a Bill Clinton, Newt Gingrich-style triangulator. So, you know, look to the states. Democrats flipped a bunch of state legislatures and will have trifectas in state governance in some key places. So while Washington maybe will be mired in inertia, it's the states that will be the incubators for policy, and we'll see how those policies are received by voters, particularly in purple and red states.KELLY: All right. That's one thing to keep an eye on. Let me do a quick lightning round and just run through what else we should be watching for as we try to make sense of what just happened. Eric?MCDANIEL: I'll let my colleagues take the serious stuff. I've got a fun one. Nonvoting members. There are more than a million Americans, like many of us who live in this city, who lack voting representation in Congress. But there's a fresh-faced class of new nonvoting members from the Virgin Islands, Guam and, yes, Washington, D.C., going to the Hill to advocate for civil rights for those they represent.KELLY: Excellent. Domenico?MONTANARO: I mean, 2028 starts now. January and February, we're going to see announcements probably for the presidency - presidential candidacies. And Trump and this Trump-lash, how is that going to reshape the Republican field? I guarantee you there's going to be more people running now than they - than who would have before.KELLY: Trump-lash. We shall watch for it. Emily, you get the last word.FENG: Two things from me. Given that the economy and gas prices are concerns for voters, the easiest way to address that would be to end the war with Iran. So will there be serious diplomatic negotiations again with Iran? And a second thing - in about two weeks, Trump heads to China. He's going to meet with the Chinese leader again, maybe even Russia's Vladimir Putin. So I'm curious, now that he's more constrained at home, will he try to make some kind of grand foreign policy bargain abroad with these heads of state?KELLY: That's NPR's Emily Feng, Eric McDaniel and Domenico Montanaro. Thanks to all three of you. Please go get some sleep now (laughter).MONTANARO: Great to be here.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: South Carolina winner Annie Andrews talks about her win and the path ahead
description: NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews, who bested Republican candidate Darline Graham, the incumbent and sister of the late S
body:
NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews, who bested Republican candidate Darline Graham, the incumbent and sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  It's a new day in many states where Democrats flipped seats, even against the odds, and including red South Carolina. Democrat and doctor, Annie Andrews, will head to the U.S. Senate in January, having bested Republican candidate Darline Graham, the incumbent and the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. She joins us now. Dr. Andrews, or maybe I should say Senator-elect Andrews, welcome.ANNIE ANDREWS: Well, thank you so much for having me.KELLY: If I had told you a few years ago that South Carolina would elect to the U.S. Senate someone who is pro abortion rights, pro some gun control measures and that that person would be you, would you have believed me?ANDREWS: I definitely would not have believed the part about it being me. This was never a career path I saw for myself. I decided to be a doctor when I was 4, and I never planned to do anything other than practice pediatrics. But what I saw in the hospital for the 20 years I worked as a pediatrician in the children's hospital, it drove me to want to get involved in politics to solve the problems I was seeing in the hospital exam room.KELLY: And is that, being a pediatrician, going to inform the way you take on this new job?ANDREWS: Absolutely. You know, those stories that I will carry with me to Washington, D.C., of watching insurance companies stand between sick children and the care that they need, sitting down with parents after diagnosing their children with new chronic diseases like asthma or diabetes and watching them worry about whether or not they can afford the asthma inhaler I prescribed or the insulin I prescribed for their diabetes - these families need help. There's so many families like that across South Carolina, and I'll be fighting for them in the U.S. Senate.KELLY: So I mentioned that you beat Darline Graham to win this race. She got herself in all kinds of hot water over the summer in a debate when she said, and I quote, that she wasn't "that informed on national security." So I want to ask you, with respect, what does your learning curve look like on national security, foreign policy, all kinds of things that maybe hadn't been front and center for you as a South Carolina pediatrician?ANDREWS: Yeah, so I've done my homework my whole life. You have to do that to get into medical school and graduate from medical school. And I'm looking forward to, you know, being ready for this job on Day 1. And, you know, Darline's gaff on national security certainly set the tone for what a lot of South Carolinians thought about her. But I think the real story was South Carolina rejected the idea that Washington, D.C., was going to pick our next senator. And she really represented everything that's broken in Washington, D.C. And instead, they chose me, someone who vows to be an independent voice, to work across the aisle to solve the problems that I heard about on the campaign trail for the past 18 months.KELLY: I saw Nikki Haley, the Republican former governor of your state. She said last night South Carolina didn't vote for you. They voted against Trump Republicans. What do you think? Do you think both can be true?ANDREWS: I think we worked really hard to build a campaign that was for everyone. And we brought together people from across the political spectrum. I was so proud to earn the endorsement of former Republican South Carolina Governor David Beasley, also proud to have the support of Ralph Norman's children, including his son, Warren Norman. And we built a campaign that was really laser-focused on the problems South Carolinians face, regardless of if you're a Republican, a Democrat or an independent.And that's what the story from last night was - that people are tired of the divisiveness. They're more concerned about what's happening in South Carolina than they are about the party politics in Washington, D.C. And they saw in me someone who will be a fighter for South Carolina, someone who's serious about solving these problems and, again, willing to work across the aisle. The only two senators I've talked to since I won my race last night are Senators Darline Graham and Senator Tim Scott. And Tim Scott and I are planning to get together next week because we're going to work together to solve...KELLY: Yeah.ANDREWS: ...The problems that we're facing here in South Carolina.KELLY: Well, talk me through that. What does it actually look like to work across the aisle? And specifically, how are you thinking about working with President Trump? He has already said he plans to use his veto power aggressively.ANDREWS: I'll work with anyone who's willing to solve the problems that we're facing here. You know, in particular, with Donald Trump, I support the no tax on tips, no tax on Social Security. I've seen him do some work to lower the cost of prescription drugs. But I take my - you know, I take the same approach I took to my job as a pediatrician. You walk into a hospital room of a sick or injured child. It doesn't matter what the patient and family's background is, their political ideology, how - you know, what kind of insurance they have. You just take care of the problem in front of you. And I think that's the governing approach we need to take in Washington, D.C.So, you know, Tim Scott and I are going to be representing South Carolina together in the U.S. Senate. And today, when we talked, we discussed that we don't agree on a lot, but we agree that South Carolina needs two people in the Senate who will work to solve the problems that South Carolina is facing. So I look forward to being part of a new era of bipartisanship in Washington, D.C.KELLY: And just quickly, and God forgive me for already bringing up 2028, but the first Democratic primary of 2028 is South Carolina, your state. What do you see your role as being?ANDREWS: You know, I'm really not focused on that. We just won this race last night, and I'm really focused on building the strongest Senate office South Carolina has ever seen to deliver the best constituent services we have ever seen here in South Carolina.KELLY: Right.ANDREWS: And then my No. 1 priority in D.C. will be stopping these Medicaid budget cuts.KELLY: We will look forward to calling you back between now and 2028 and seeing how it's going. That's Annie Andrews, Democratic senator-elect in South Carolina. Thank you.ANDREWS: Thank you.

title: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms
description: Elon Musk gave more than $445 million to
body:
Elon Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings but most of the candidates he backed on Tuesday lost.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.   With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.   
   Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.   The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.   During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy nonprofit.   "The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X.   Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."   
   U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.   "How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X.   Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.   While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.   "SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.   Texas has played a growing role in Musk's business empire   Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.   Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.   
   SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced.   Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.   But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.   
   "Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," said James Talarico, who defeated Paxton in the Senate race, at a campaign rally in Lubbock last month.   Elon Musk's own posts on X about Talarico were often personal and incendiary. "Talarico will vote to trans your kids," he wrote on Nov. 1.   Talarico addressed Musk in his victory speech on Tuesday.   "We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country. Power belongs to the people," Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not right versus left; it is top versus bottom."   As results came in on Tuesday night, Musk wrote on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," followed by a shrug emoji.

title: Rahm Emanuel maps out a vision for what Democrats can achieve after taking Congress
description: NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former congressman and Obama advisor Rahm Emanuel about what Democrats' strategy should be, now that they'll soon
body:
NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former congressman and Obama advisor Rahm Emanuel about what Democrats' strategy should be, now that they'll soon control both houses of Congress.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  The blue tsunami that swept Democrats into control of both houses of Congress will give the party new power to check President Trump for the last two years of his term. So what should the priorities of Democrats be, and how much can they expect to actually accomplish? We're going to put those questions to Democrat Rahm Emanuel now. He served as Chicago's mayor, a congressional representative and chief of staff to President Obama. Welcome.RAHM EMANUEL: Thank you. How are you?CHANG: Very good. I wanted to ask you about something that you said last night during NPR's Special Coverage of election night. You told my co-host Scott Detrow that voters have given Democrats a, quote, "second look" that they haven't gotten in the past.EMANUEL: That's right.CHANG: Well, now that Democrats have won that second look, what is the Day 1 agenda?EMANUEL: Well, one is you have to look at this. This was a repudiation of the Republicans, not a vindication of us. We have a second look. We have a broad, what I call, electoral coalition. Our goal and mission now is to make it a governing coalition, and that means delivering change. What does that look like?CHANG: Yeah.EMANUEL: One, comprehensive lobbying reform for all three branches of government. Power wash the place - a ban on all stock trading, a ban on all participation in prediction markets, a mandatory retirement or term limits, a mandatory blind trust and then the Kushner rule, which is you can't take foreign investments and money while you're in government and for two years afterwards. Two, while prices are up, what hasn't gone up? The minimum wage in 20 years.CHANG: Yeah.EMANUEL: Raise the minimum wage. And then third and finally - if not third - there's two other things (ph) - restrict and repeal many of the tariffs. And then, fourth, restore some of the healthcare cuts that were done on Medicaid and on the ACA exchange...CHANG: OK.EMANUEL: ...So people get healthcare in America.CHANG: OK, you've just cited a number of ideas that Democrats can tackle over the next two years. But the question on a lot of people's minds is, can Democrats speak with a more unified voice?EMANUEL: (Laughter).CHANG: Both moderate and progressive Democrats were elected last night.EMANUEL: Sure.CHANG: You have been critical of progressive politics, issues that center on identity. Can the progressives and the moderates within the Democratic caucuses work together, you think?EMANUEL: So two things. One is, I have been critical because in our successful efforts, we have worked to find things like economic security, education, things that bring people together. Identity politics actually divide people and break them off rather than finding unifying economic values and social values that unite. Now I do that having worked with both President Obama and President Clinton. Their success wasn't figuring out how to divide the country, but it was actually how to unite the country. You know, if you do identity politics, the other side gets to do identity politics.CHANG: Sure.EMANUEL: And there's more identity there, so it's a bad strategy and...CHANG: But do you think Hakeem Jeffries...EMANUEL: ...Bad for the country.CHANG: Do you think Hakeem Jeffries, presumably, potentially the next speaker of the House, do you think he can effectively bridge the fault lines that are running through the Democratic caucus right now in the House? I mean, 'cause...EMANUEL: Yeah.CHANG: ...Speaker Pelosi, I mean, she managed to navigate a lot of complicated fissures in her party back then, but...EMANUEL: I have - yes, I - so the short answer is yes, because he has a - the count's still going on, but he has a significant majority where no one element can hold him hostage. What has happened to the Republican speakers of late is that they were held hostage by three members. When you have 200, call it, I'll just, for this show, 45 or more, you can tell nine members, make sure the door doesn't hit you on the way out. They can't hold the team hostage. That gives you massive leverage.CHANG: So the math is on Jeffries' side, is what you're saying, the math inside (inaudible).EMANUEL: No doubt about it. No doubt about it. Now, the other thing I used to say, you know, look, as a - I (laughter) - I'm saying a joke, and then I realize I'm on NPR, so I better not say it.CHANG: (Laughter).EMANUEL: I used to (inaudible) Nancy Pelosi.CHANG: Go ahead.EMANUEL: Mo Udall had this great line, a former caucus chair. And I was  - when we were trying to count votes, the speaker and I, I said, remember what Mo Udall used to say, and she would look up. I said, what's the difference between a cactus and a caucus? In a cactus, the pricks are on the outside.CHANG: (Laughter).EMANUEL: So OK? That was Mo Udall, not me. Nancy used to laugh, also. But, look, you got to basically - I'll give you an example. Let's just tease this out. You're going to have, appropriately, hearings about all the corruption. But the hearings aren't going to change. You have a choice. If you do impeachment, the coalition that elected you are going to say, eh, it's just more of the same. You do an ethics bill, they're going to say, that's a change I voted for. You got to think about the Kansas senator. You got to think about Nancy Lacore in the Charleston, South Carolina, district that flipped that district. You got to think about Sean McCann, who just won by 300 votes in western Michigan.CHANG: OK. Wait, let me make sure I understand what you are saying, because there are a lot of Democrats...EMANUEL: I was speaking in English.(LAUGHTER)CHANG: Let me make sure that I understand what you're saying. A lot of Democrats are actually quite eager in the House...EMANUEL: Yeah.CHANG: ...To start investigations. In fact, the incoming House oversight chair, Robert Garcia...EMANUEL: I'm for that.CHANG: ...Posted on social media last night, lawyer up. I'm assuming he's directing that message to Republicans. Do you worry - is - what you're saying is that you are concerned Democrats could put too much focus on investigating the Trump administration...EMANUEL: No, that's not what I said. So let me...CHANG: ...And their allies and not delivering policies...EMANUEL: No, no, no.CHANG: ...That voters actually want?EMANUEL: I'll slow down. I'm all for the hearings. Follow the money.CHANG: OK.EMANUEL: But you better - the hearings are not the end in themselves. They're a means towards lobbying and ethics reform. If you don't finish it, you'll have fallen short. You need...CHANG: Do you think Democrats should try to impeach President Trump a third time?EMANUEL: As I said, lobbying and ethics reform, no. Let me, just by way of reference - in 2007, led the effort in '06 to make Nancy speaker, take the majority. Senator Obama, John McCain, Russ Feingold, and in the House, myself, Marty Meehan and Chris Shays, we passed the last major lobbying and ethics reform 20 years ago. Use the majority and then what happens a year later? President Obama gets elected. OK, use the majority to make real change, make the coalition that elected that change, be a governing coalition and deliver.CHANG: What I hear you saying is, go ahead, investigate away, but make sure that you get things done as well.EMANUEL: Here's...CHANG: Let me ask you one more thing 'cause I know you only have a few minutes with us. Given that you feel that way, how much of a risk do you think there is that voters will hold Democrats responsible in 2028 if the economy doesn't turn around?EMANUEL: Well, in that case, they mainly hold the president, historically. Our job is to deliver change with speed. And I mean that with speed. As I always like to say, the first eight letters of progressive is progress, not perfection. Raise the minimum wage, restrict the tariffs, pass lobbying and ethics reform bill, and then the people that elected you said, you know what? You're different. You're not more of the same. You're actual change. This was a change election, a repudiation. Now we have to turn in - not spike the ball on the 20 yard line, but actually deliver the touchdown that the American people want.CHANG: Well, you mentioned the presidential aspect of the election in 2028. There's no secret that you are personally exploring a run for president. Do last night's results push your decision one way or the other?EMANUEL: No.CHANG: What is your decision?EMANUEL: To get off this interview.(LAUGHTER)CHANG: Fair enough. It's been lovely to talk to you. Rahm Emanuel - he's held a number of Democratic leadership positions, including Mayor of Chicago and White House Chief of Staff. Thank you so much.EMANUEL: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF JONUFF'S "CROW")

title: Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
description: Voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballo
body:
Voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures across dozens of states.
                
                    Mario Tama/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mario Tama/Getty Images
    

   
   Tuesday's midterm elections were a huge sweep for Democrats, among other takeaways.   And across 39 states — plus Washington, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands — voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures spanning issues from taxes to transgender rights to traffic cameras to data centers and AI.   Here's a look at some of those results.   Three states moved to preserve abortion access    The U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, leaving the legality and regulation of abortion up to each state. In subsequent elections, over a dozen states have put access to abortion on their ballots — and overwhelmingly moved to secure it.   
   This year, four states considered abortion measures. Three passed, while Idaho voted to preserve the state's abortion ban from 2022.   In Missouri, voters rejected a Republican-led amendment that would have banned abortion with few exceptions. The move affirms support for abortion just two years after voters mobilized to reject Missouri's ban, which was one of the strictest in the country.   
   Nevada residents voted to enshrine abortion up to the point of viability in their constitution. They did so for the second election in a row, since state law requires a proposed constitutional amendment to pass twice.   Virginians voted to create a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" in their constitution. That includes the right to an abortion during the first two trimesters (and afterward in certain cases), as well as the right to contraception, fertility, postpartum care and more.   States voted on voting    Many states considered changes to how they run their elections.   It was too early to call Wednesday afternoon whether voters had approved some of the more far-reaching changes, in Alaska and Arizona.   Other states — including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio — passed measures toughening identification requirements for voters, while California voted against such an effort.   Several states — including Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia — approved measures reinforcing that U.S. citizenship is required to vote in their elections.   
   Redistricting was also top of mind for voters. President Trump kicked off a redistricting race earlier this year by urging Republican-led states to redraw their districts ahead of the midterms. Republicans and Democrats in multiple states did so. But many of the districts altered to boost GOP prospects ultimately went to Democratic candidates.   Missouri voters rejected a Republican-friendly congressional map, while Maryland voters passed a redistricting amendment that could pave the way for a Democrat-leaning map in 2028.   
   Virginians passed a measure automatically restoring voting rights to anyone convicted of a felony once they have completed their sentence.   A mixed bag for LGBTQ rights    Virginians also passed a constitutional amendment officially repealing its ban on gay marriage and adding language confirming that the commonwealth will recognize marriage between two adults regardless of their sex, gender or race.   Virginia's ban has been moot since the Supreme Court made same-sex marriage legal nationwide in 2015, but this measure is seen as a safeguard in case Obergefell v. Hodges gets reversed (as some have feared in the wake of the court's overturning of Roe v. Wade). Other states have made similar moves, including Colorado and California in 2024.   Vermont overwhelmingly voted to add an amendment to its constitution guaranteeing equal protection under the law "race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin."   A number of states considered measures restricting transgender kids' access to school sports teams and gender-affirming care, with Colorado passing both. A Washington state measure to ban trans students from competing in girls' school sports was still leading on Wednesday.   Arizona passed a proposal requiring schools and athletic associations to restrict students, athletes and employees from using facilities — including restrooms, locker rooms, and other private spaces — that are not designated for their sex assigned at birth. Arizona law already bans trans girls from playing on school sports teams designated for girls, and this measure would extend that prohibition to recreational organizations like Little League.   
   Taxes and state spending up for debate     One of the most high-profile ballot measures asked Floridians to weigh cutting property taxes for homeowners, which critics say would take billions of dollars in local government revenue away from much-needed public services like food banks, libraries, transportation and infrastructure. Voters overwhelmingly passed the amendment.   In California, voters pondered whether to approve a one-off 5% tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets, with most of the money raised going toward health care services. The fight against that ballot measure was one of the most expensive in the state's history. The contest is too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon.   
   Tennessee voters approved a constitutional amendment prohibiting its government from levying a statewide property tax, which it has not collected since 1949. Arizona voters passed a measure that bans cities and towns from raising taxes on groceries until July 2027. North Carolinians approved an amendment to cap the maximum personal income tax at 3.5%.   Washington voters considered whether to repeal an income tax on individuals and households earning more than $1 million, which is scheduled to take effect in 2028. Early results indicate they want to keep that tax.   A polar-opposite pair of gun ballot measures    Massachusetts voted to keep a 2024 law tightening firearm regulations. The law made Massachusetts gun control measures among the strictest in the nation, as it also included requiring "ghost guns" to have a serial number, broadened the definition of "assault-style firearm" and expanded the state's red flag laws.   Meanwhile, in Idaho, a ballot measure asked voters for help choosing the official state gun from six different brands and models. The Winchester Model 1873 — aka the "Gun that Won the West" — leads in the polls as of Wednesday, though the state legislature would need to pass a separate law to make the winner official.   
   The ballot initiatives about data centers    At least 38 jurisdictions voted on the sprawling facilities needed to power AI, and Tuesday revealed how many voters dislike them. Jurisdictions in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin voted to restrict data centers.   Of these, at least 12 localities voted to restrict the size of data centers, while six others voted to halt development and ban construction of all facilities, according to Data Centers on the Ballot.   The one community that supported data centers is in Harwood, North Dakota, where 75% of voters did not want to place restrictions on industrial projects, including data centers.   Ohio, one of the frontline states on the issue, had 21 ballot measures mentioning data centers. Voters there moved to restrict the AI facilities: Trenton, Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25 megawatts, while Hubbard moved to ban construction of data centers of any size, including converting existing buildings. Ohio voters also rejected rezoning areas from rural residential to light industrial for data center usage.   Candidates spent up to $40 million on ads about data centers this election cycle. They were a contentious issue in many statewide elections, as 77% of Americans say they are concerned about data centers raising electricity costs, according to a June Reuters/Ipsos poll. The poll also showed two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans said they'd oppose a data center in their community.   Other honorable mentions    Alabama voters passed ballot measures requiring local school boards to adopt policies directing public K-12 schools to recite the Pledge of Allegiance and, separately, play or perform the first stanza of "The Star-Spangled Banner" at least once a week during school hours.   In Arizona, voters passed a measure banning the state from installing and using photo enforcement systems (like speed and red-light cameras) to catch people who violate certain traffic ordinances.   
   Residents of Washington, D.C. had just one ballot initiative to consider: banning the controversial duck or goose liver dish known as foie gras. The debate went viral in recent days, prompting a slew of Halloween costumes, a four-course restaurant tasting menu and public appearances by a real duck named Olivia. D.C. voted overwhelmingly to prohibit the force-feeding of birds to enlarge their livers, and the sale of the delicacy itself. Across the country, voters in Denver approved a similar measure.

title: It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
description: Dr. Annie Andrews, who won the race for
body:
Dr. Annie Andrews, who won the race for Senate in South Carolina, talked about the measles outbreak in the state in her campaign. She's pictured at an election night party in Charleston.
                
                    Mic Smith/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mic Smith/AP
    

   
   The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.   Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.   Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.   In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.   
   Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.   "I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.   
   "It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.   Blue wins, red losses   In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)   
   In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.   A big recruiting effort   Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.   The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.   "We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.   Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton at her victory party in Columbus, Ohio.
                
                    Carolyn Kaster/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Carolyn Kaster/AP
    

   
   Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.   "People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."   
   A key vote, a damaging investigation   Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.   During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."   Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., speaks before President Donald Trump at a campaign rally at the Salina Regional Airport, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina Kan.

   In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.   All the way back to 1776   Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.   
   "In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."   In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."   The new count   To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.   In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.   In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.   
   Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."   He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says   
   A health policy shake up?   Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.   
   Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.   "I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."   Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.   "I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."   Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

schema.headline: It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
